what: The control for Sarrus Lift. It is the same 144-piece lift with one change: the passive chain B, the hinged pair of links whose axes are perpendicular to the driven chain A, is removed (9 parts). Motor A only holds its saved angle; nothing is driven. In the simulator the deck cannot stay where it is: within a second it sinks about 45 mm, tilts about 50° and slides about 20 mm sideways. In the full Sarrus Lift, held the same way, the deck stays exactly level and in place.
try: Load the full Sarrus Lift first and look at its two link chains under the deck: their hinge axes point in perpendicular directions.
Load this control, press Reset, then Run, and watch the deck as soon as the lab starts. Chain A still holds one edge, but the deck swings down and tips.
Look along chain A's hinge axes. The deck turns about a line parallel to them: that is the one motion chain A cannot stop.
Compare with Sarrus Lift: there chain B blocks exactly that rotation and that sideways slide, so only straight up-and-down motion is left.
why: A chain of links joined by parallel hinges can only move in one plane, but inside that plane it allows the deck to tilt and slide as well as rise. Chain A alone therefore leaves the deck free to rotate about an axis parallel to its hinges and to shift sideways, and gravity uses that freedom at once. Chain B on its own would allow the same kind of motion in the perpendicular plane. Only together do they leave one shared motion: the deck moves straight up and down and stays level. That is Pierre-Frédéric Sarrus's 1853 discovery, the first exact straight-line linkage with only hinges and no sliding guide.
matters: Straight-line motion without rails mattered in the 19th century because accurate slideways were hard to make, and it still matters wherever sliding guides would jam, wear or collect dirt: scissor-like lifting tables, folding mechanisms and deployable space structures. The control shows a general design rule: every degree of freedom you do not want has to be blocked by some part of the mechanism. If one chain is missing, the motion it was blocking appears at once.
question: With only chain A, the deck tips and slides. Which motions does chain B block in the full Sarrus Lift, and which single motion is left?
answer: Chain A allows the deck to rotate about an axis parallel to its hinges and to slide in its plane. Chain B, with perpendicular hinges, blocks exactly those motions, and chain A blocks the corresponding motions of chain B. The only motion both chains allow is straight vertical translation of a level deck.
further: Count degrees of freedom: a free rigid deck has six. How many does each hinge chain remove, and why do the two chains together leave exactly one?
What would happen if chain B were rebuilt with its hinges parallel to chain A instead of perpendicular?
Why is the motor held at its saved angle in this control instead of driving the lift as in Sarrus Lift?
formula: Full Sarrus Lift: deck level, Δh = 96[sin(45° + A/24) − sin 45°] mm. Single chain A: the deck keeps a free rotation about an axis parallel to chain A's hinges, so it tips and slides under gravity (in the simulator about 45 mm down, 50° tilt, 20 mm sideways).
